title: Principles for Prompt Engineering - Karina Nguyen (Claude Instant @ Anthropic)

primary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming
primary.rationale: The entire talk is about prompt engineering principles and techniques: six writing principles (clarity, conciseness, coherence, consistency, direction, grounding), XML-tagged structured output with near-100% formatting accuracy, chain-of-thought prompting with thought tags and scoring, decomposition-based prompting for complex questions, few-shot patterns, self-consistency via majority voting, and API formatting best practices (Human/Assistant structure, putting words in Claude's mouth, hedging, direct quotes). These map directly to the inclusion criteria: 'Primary focus is prompts, structured generation, or LLM-as-program patterns.'

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: A substantial section covers Claude's 100K context window, instruction placement at the end versus beginning of prompts, the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon, and long-context document Q&A with measured accuracy differences. This maps to the inclusion criteria about context construction and engineering the working set the model sees.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: The talk dedicates a section to evaluation methodology: generating QA pairs from government documents, testing instruction placement effectiveness, measuring thought tag impact on accuracy, and comparing Claude 2 versus Claude Instant performance differences. Auto-labeling quality assessment via clustering is also covered.

secondary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
secondary.rationale: Red teaming and jailbreak robustness is discussed in the Q&A, including Claude Instant's specific training for red teaming resistance and the expectation that the model refuses unsafe prompts. This is a minor topic rather than a primary focus of the talk.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The prompt engineering principles, XML structuring, chain-of-thought techniques, and API formatting tips are cross-domain and not tied to a specific application vertical. The talk teaches generalizable principles applicable to any LLM-based product.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk is aimed at developers and engineers building with LLMs, covering API formatting, prompt design patterns, evaluation methodology, and practical deployment considerations like choosing between Claude 2 and Claude Instant.

domains.label: Search & Knowledge
domains.rationale: The Inalia case study uses CLIP embeddings for multimodal clothing search via cosine similarity, and the auto-labeling section covers UMAP dimensionality reduction and K-means clustering for knowledge organization. These touch on search and knowledge topics but are illustrative examples rather than the core focus.

summary: Karina Nguyen, an engineer at Anthropic who worked on Claude's post-training, model behavior research, and early products including claude.ai, presents prompt engineering principles at the AI Engineer Summit 2023. She frames prompting as increasing the probability of desired outputs via attention mechanisms that activate relevant internal knowledge, comparing it to creative writing requiring hypothesis formation, assumption testing, and iteration. Six writing principles—clarity, conciseness, coherence, consistency, direction, and grounding—guide prompt construction. Claude should be treated like a human, explained to elaborately, and strongly prefers XML tags for structuring prompts (the first format it was fine-tuned on), yielding near-100% formatting accuracy. A recommendation system case study (project Inalia) demonstrates zero-shot and chain-of-thought techniques with XML tags, explicit criteria, and 1-10 scoring using CLIP for multimodal search. She addresses Claude's 100K context window, finding that chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful—the model may not attend to its own stated reasoning—and introduces decomposition-based methods that break complex questions into independent sub-questions answered separately then recomposed. Evaluation methodology demonstrates using Claude to generate QA pairs from government documents, with placing instructions at the end of prompts and using thought tags improving accuracy. The talk covers auto-labeling via UMAP embeddings and K-means clustering, self-consistency through majority voting, and API formatting best practices including strict Human/Assistant structure, putting words in Claude's mouth, hedging, and requesting direct quotes. The talk concludes with the future of prompt engineering including synthetic data generation, AI feedback (RLAIF), and self-revision. Final Q&A covers title generation in production, Claude 2 versus Claude Instant differences (Claude 2 is larger and smarter; Claude Instant is cheaper, faster, specifically trained for math, code, and red teaming), and red teaming robustness against jailbreaks.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a cohesive framework for building production LLM systems. The foundational AI concepts—next-token probability estimation and attention mechanisms—explain why prompt engineering works at a mechanistic level, while the chain-of-thought faithfulness finding reveals its limitations. The six writing principles and XML tag structuring provide the practical engineering layer for translating these theoretical insights into reliable, parseable outputs. Decomposition-based prompting bridges AI theory and software architecture by offering a pattern for handling complex reasoning where chain-of-thought is unfaithful. The evaluation methodology closes the loop by enabling systematic measurement of whether prompt changes actually improve performance, while anti-hallucination strategies and API formatting conventions address production reliability concerns. The Claude 2 vs Claude Instant comparison and red teaming discussion connect these techniques to real model deployment decisions, showing how model-specific training differences affect which strategies to apply. The production title generation example demonstrates the full lifecycle—from choosing when to invoke the LLM at all, to using editorial context for consistency, to cost-aware heuristics. Together, these concepts demonstrate that effective prompt engineering is not merely writing instructions but a full engineering discipline requiring attention to model internals, structured output design, evaluation infrastructure, and production safety.
temporalContext: The talk was delivered at the AI Engineer Summit 2023 in San Francisco on October 20, 2023. At the time, Claude 2 (announced August 9, 2023) and Claude Instant were the current Anthropic models. The CoT faithfulness paper was published July 18, 2023, and the decomposition paper was submitted July 17, 2023, both shortly before the talk. The talk predates Claude 3 (released March 2024) and all subsequent model generations. Karina Nguyen was still employed at Anthropic at the time of the talk; she later joined OpenAI. The prompt engineering practices and API conventions described reflect the state of the Claude API and tooling as of late 2023. Research verification was conducted as of August 23, 2026, confirming that model-specific details may have evolved while the general principles remain applicable.

concepts.name: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
concepts.explanation: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful—the model may not attend to its own stated reasoning when producing final answers. This was documented in an Anthropic research paper co-authored by the speaker, finding that as models become larger, they may produce less faithful reasoning.
concepts.importance: Challenges the assumption that visible reasoning steps reflect the model's actual decision process, with direct implications for trust, interpretability, and safety in deployed systems.

concepts.name: Next-Token Probability and Attention Mechanisms
concepts.explanation: Language models estimate the probability of each subsequent word given preceding words. Effective prompts leverage attention mechanisms to activate relevant internal knowledge. Prompting is fundamentally about increasing the probability of desired outputs through careful input design.
concepts.importance: Provides the theoretical foundation for why prompt engineering works, connecting prompt design choices to model internals rather than treating prompting as a black art.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Classification with Scoring
concepts.explanation: The recommendation case study demonstrates replacing binary yes/no classification with a 1-10 scoring scale, with critique reasoning in thought tags. Zero-shot prompting uses XML tags for structured output without requiring labeled examples, achieving richer signal than binary decisions.
concepts.importance: Shows how prompt design choices (scoring scale vs binary, thought tags for reasoning) directly affect the quality and granularity of model outputs in classification tasks.

concepts.name: Long Context Window and Instruction Placement
concepts.explanation: Claude's 100K context window enables processing entire books for multi-document summarization or large few-shot prompts. For long-context document Q&A, placing instructions at the end of the prompt significantly outperforms placing them at the beginning, likely because the model attends more to the end of the prompt due to distance.
concepts.importance: Reveals that context engineering—how and where information is positioned within the prompt—has measurable effects on model performance, informing prompt design for long-context applications.

concepts.name: Claude 2 vs Claude Instant Model Differences
concepts.explanation: Claude 2 is a larger, smarter model; Claude Instant is cheaper, faster, and specifically trained for math, code, and red teaming robustness. Claude Instant benefited more from prompt optimizations than Claude 2, suggesting that larger models are more robust to suboptimal prompting.
concepts.importance: Informs model selection decisions in production based on cost, latency, task type, and the importance of prompt engineering effort, directly affecting deployment economics.

concepts.name: Red Teaming and Jailbreak Robustness
concepts.explanation: Red teaming evaluates model robustness against jailbreaks—prompts designed to elicit unsafe behavior such as bomb-making instructions. The model is expected to refuse such prompts. Claude Instant was specifically trained for greater robustness against red teaming attacks.
concepts.importance: Connects prompt engineering to AI safety: understanding how models can be manipulated through prompts is essential for deploying safe, reliable LLM systems.

concepts.name: XML Tag Structured Prompting
concepts.explanation: Using XML tags to structure prompts and constrain output format with Claude. XML was the first format Claude was fine-tuned on, yielding near-100% formatting accuracy compared to markdown or JSON. Tags also suppress unwanted preamble by constraining output structure.
concepts.importance: Directly determines output reliability and parseability in production systems; incorrect formatting choices cause cascading downstream failures in automated pipelines.

concepts.name: Claude API Human/Assistant Formatting
concepts.explanation: Strict Human/Assistant formatting with proper newlines is critical for Claude API performance. Missing or incorrect formatting produces very poor results. These special words should never be doubled or placed inside XML context tags.
concepts.importance: Essential for correct API integration; errors here cause catastrophic output degradation that is difficult to diagnose without knowing this convention.

concepts.name: Iterative Prompt Development Methodology
concepts.explanation: Prompt engineering is framed as creative writing requiring hypothesis formation, assumption testing, and iteration. Six writing principles—clarity, conciseness, coherence, consistency, direction, grounding—guide prompt construction with context first and task last. Claude should be treated like a human, explained to as if to a five-year-old.
concepts.importance: Establishes prompt engineering as a disciplined engineering practice rather than ad-hoc trial and error, providing a repeatable methodology for teams building LLM-based products.

concepts.name: LLM Evaluation Methodology
concepts.explanation: Using Claude to generate multiple-choice QA pairs from documents to create evaluation datasets, then measuring accuracy across different prompt configurations. Key finding: placing instructions at the end of the prompt significantly outperforms placing them at the beginning for long-context document Q&A.
concepts.importance: Without systematic evaluation, prompt changes cannot be validated; this methodology provides a reproducible framework for measuring LLM performance on specific tasks before deployment.

concepts.name: Anti-Hallucination Prompting Strategies
concepts.explanation: Techniques include letting Claude hedge with 'I don't know' or 'I don't have enough information,' requesting direct quotes from documents with fallback statements, and putting words in Claude's mouth to anchor understanding. These reduce fabrication in production systems.
concepts.importance: Directly addresses one of the most critical production risks with LLMs—fabricated information—through actionable prompt-level mitigations that require no model changes.

concepts.name: Decomposition-Based Prompting Architecture
concepts.explanation: Breaking complex questions into independent, self-contained sub-questions answered in separate contexts (potentially by different models), then recomposed into a final answer. This reduces step-to-step bias and improves faithfulness compared to chain-of-thought, where the model may not attend to its own stated reasoning.
concepts.importance: Provides an architectural pattern for handling complex multi-step reasoning in production systems where reasoning faithfulness and auditability matter.

concepts.name: Production Title Generation with Context
concepts.explanation: In production, title generation for Claude AI used Claude as an editor with editorial taste, placing previous titles in context for stylistic consistency. Short prompts bypassed the LLM entirely, using the first words of the conversation as a heuristic.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a real production pattern for LLM-based feature engineering, including cost-aware heuristic optimization that bypasses the model when unnecessary.

sections.title: Introduction and Why Prompting Is Hard
sections.summary: Karina introduces herself and her work on Claude at Anthropic. She explains that models estimate next-word probabilities using attention mechanisms, and effective prompts activate relevant internal knowledge. Prompting is hard for three reasons: users can't elicit best performance, users vaguely know their needs, or users don't know what they want. She compares prompting to creative writing, requiring hypothesis formation, assumption testing, and iteration.

sections.title: Writing Principles for Claude
sections.summary: Six writing principles are introduced: clarity, conciseness, coherence, consistency, direction, and grounding. Claude should be treated like a human, explained to as if to a five-year-old. Claude strongly prefers XML tags, originally fine-tuned on XML before learning markdown and JSON from customer needs. Consistent formatting prevents putting the model off distribution.

sections.title: Case Study: Recommendation System with CLIP and Claude
sections.summary: The Inalia project uses CLIP for multimodal clothing search via image-text embeddings and cosine similarity. Claude curates recommendations by classifying item relevance to user queries. Two strategies are demonstrated: zero-shot with XML tags, and chain-of-thought with thought tags and explicit criteria. XML tags also help suppress unwanted preamble by constraining output format.

sections.title: Recommendation Scoring and Q&A
sections.summary: The recommendation system is refined by replacing binary yes/no with a 1-10 scoring scale inside score tags, with critique reasoning in thought tags. Q&A addresses why non-native English prompts still work well (models infer intent probabilistically) and whether score distributions show bias, which is noted as active research within Anthropic's societal impacts group.

sections.title: Long Context and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
sections.summary: Claude's 100K context window enables processing entire books. Long context can be used for multi-document summarization or huge few-shot prompts. A recent Anthropic paper finds chain-of-thought is not always faithful—the model may not attend to its own stated reasoning when producing final answers. Decomposition-based methods can match chain-of-thought performance on QA while improving faithfulness.

sections.title: Decomposition-Based Prompting
sections.summary: Decomposition breaks a complex question into independent, self-contained sub-questions, each answered in isolation (potentially by different models), then recomposed into a final answer. This reduces bias from step-to-step influence. A legal multiple-choice QA example demonstrates the technique: the model first generates numbered sub-questions in XML tags, each is answered separately, and all answers are combined for the final response.

sections.title: Evaluating Long-Context Recall
sections.summary: Anthropic evaluated Claude's long-context recall by using Claude to generate multiple-choice QA pairs from government meeting transcripts dated after Claude's training cutoff. Documents were split into sections, with five questions generated per section. Results show that placing instructions at the end of the prompt significantly outperforms placing them at the beginning, and using thought tags for reasoning improves accuracy. Claude Instant benefited more from these optimizations than Claude 2.

sections.title: Q&A on Instruction Placement and XML vs Markdown
sections.summary: Q&A addresses why placing instructions at the end works better—the hypothesis is that the model attends more to the end of the prompt due to distance. The 'lost in the middle' paper does not apply to Claude for long-context Q&A. XML tags yield almost 100% accuracy versus markdown or JSON formatting.

sections.title: Auto-Labeling with Clustering and Self-Consistency
sections.summary: Language models can auto-label clusters by embedding text with UMAP, applying K-means clustering, and asking the model to generate category labels for each cluster. Self-consistency improves results by generating N independent samples and using majority voting, especially for quantitative tasks. To improve categorization when Claude misses nuance, add contrasting conceptual distinctions, bad examples, diverse few-shot examples, analogies, and common misconception corrections.

sections.title: API Formatting Tips and Anti-Hallucination Strategies
sections.summary: Key API tips include strict Human/Assistant formatting with newlines, never doubling or placing these special words inside XML context tags. Put words in Claude's mouth to anchor understanding. Let Claude hedge with 'I don't know' to reduce hallucination. Request direct quotes from documents with fallback statements. Good few-shot examples should be similar, diverse, and equally distributed among answer types.

sections.title: Future of Prompt Engineering and Q&A
sections.summary: Prompt engineering will persist as tasks become more complex. Trends include synthetic data generation, models writing evaluations, RLAIF, self-reflection and revision, and prompt engineering becoming standard in product development. Resources include Anthropic's cookbook, prompt design guide, and research paper appendices. Q&A covers differences from GPT, self-correction limitations, and evaluation methods ranging from manual review to automated refusal categorization.

sections.title: Final Q&A: Title Generation, Claude 2 vs Instant, and Red Teaming
sections.summary: Karina addresses OpenAI function calling, noting she hasn't extensively used it. She describes production title generation for Claude AI: using Claude as an editor with editorial taste, placing previous titles in context for stylistic consistency, and skipping the LLM for short prompts by using the first words. Claude 2 (announced August 9th) is larger and smarter; Claude Instant is cheaper, faster, specifically trained for math and code, and more robust against jailbreaks in red teaming. Training involved fine-tuning. Red teaming evaluates model robustness to unsafe prompts like bomb-making instructions, with the model expected to refuse; details are in the Claude 2 model card.

organization.name: Anthropic
organization.summary: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company founded in 2021, headquartered in San Francisco, California. It develops Claude, an AI assistant and frontier model family including Claude 2 and Claude Instant. The company focuses on building reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. At the time of the video (October 2023), Anthropic employed the speaker Karina Nguyen, who worked on Claude post-training, model behavior research (honesty, harmlessness, reducing hallucinations), and early products including claude.ai. Anthropic's official documentation, research papers, cookbook, and prompt engineering tutorial are referenced throughout the talk as resources. The company is privately held and active as of August 2026.
organization.status: Active — privately held AI safety and research company. Headquartered in San Francisco, CA. Products include Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. Founders include Dario Amodei (CEO), Daniela Amodei (President), and others. Approximately 3,400 employees as of mid-2026.

technologies.label: Claude Model Family
technologies.summary: The Claude model family, developed by Anthropic, is the central technology of the talk. Karina Nguyen presents prompt engineering principles specifically for Claude, covering its unique preferences for XML tags (the first format it was fine-tuned on, yielding near-100% formatting accuracy), strict Human/Assistant API formatting, and behavioral characteristics (treat like a human, explain to a five-year-old). Claude 2 (announced August 9, 2023) is positioned as larger and smarter, while Claude Instant is cheaper, faster, and specifically trained for math, code, and red teaming robustness. The talk also describes a production title generation feature using Claude as an editor with previous titles for stylistic consistency, and discusses red teaming expectations where the model should refuse unsafe prompts.
technologies.role: Central platform and model family discussed throughout the entire talk; all techniques and case studies are Claude-specific

technologies.label: XML Tag Structured Prompting
technologies.summary: XML tag structured prompting is Claude preferred prompt formatting technique, yielding near-100% formatting accuracy versus markdown or JSON. XML was the first format Claude was fine-tuned on. Tags constrain output format, suppress unwanted preamble, and enable reliable parsing in production systems. The technique encompasses thought tags for structured reasoning, scoring tags for classification, and strict Human/Assistant API formatting. Six writing principles (clarity, conciseness, coherence, consistency, direction, grounding) provide the methodological framework, with context placed first and task last. Anti-hallucination strategies including hedging and direct quote requests complement the formatting approach.
technologies.role: Primary formatting technique advocated across all prompt examples, case studies, and API best practices

technologies.label: Chain-of-Thought Prompting and Decomposition
technologies.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting guides models to reason step-by-step before producing final answers using thought tags. The talk reveals a critical limitation documented in Anthropic research co-authored by the speaker: CoT is not always faithful. The model may not attend to its own stated reasoning when producing final answers, and this problem can worsen with larger models. Decomposition-based methods address this by breaking complex questions into independent, self-contained sub-questions answered in separate contexts (potentially by different models), then recomposed into a final answer. This approach greatly increases faithfulness while achieving comparable or improved performance on QA tasks.
technologies.role: Major research theme with both theoretical limitations (CoT unfaithfulness) and practical alternatives (decomposition) presented with a legal QA case study

technologies.label: Long-Context Document Q&A
technologies.summary: Claude 100K token context window enables processing entire books for document Q&A, multi-document summarization, and large few-shot prompts. The talk demonstrates through systematic evaluation that placing instructions at the end of the prompt significantly outperforms placing them at the beginning for document Q&A, likely because the model attends more to the end of the prompt. Evaluation methodology uses Claude to generate QA pairs from government documents dated after Claude training cutoff (70K and 95K token documents), with findings that thought tags improve accuracy and Claude Instant benefited more from prompt optimizations than Claude 2. The lost in the middle phenomenon is noted as not applying to Claude for long-context Q&A.
technologies.role: Applied technique section demonstrating context engineering, instruction placement optimization, and systematic evaluation methodology for long-context recall on 70K and 95K token documents
